label: minimal dialect
citation: Steele, G. L., Jr. & Gabriel, R. P. (1993). The Evolution of Lisp. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: The initial report on Scheme [Sussman, 1975b] describes a very spare language, with a minimum of primitive constructs, one per concept.
note: Steele co-designed Scheme; the URL is a course mirror of the paper (dreamsongs.com copy is robots-blocked). R7RS (standards.scheme.org/official/r7rs.pdf) also says: 'Scheme is a statically scoped and properly tail recursive dialect of the Lisp programming language invented by Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman.'

label: Lisp dialect: code as data, macros
citation: Hickey, R. (2020). A History of Clojure. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), 1-46.
quote: Clojure is a dialect of Lisp, but is not a direct descendant of any prior Lisp.
note: Quote is from the paper's abstract (confirmed via the HOPL IV page and Crossref record for doi:10.1145/3386321; the full PDF returned 403). Clojure is a new Lisp, not a descendant of an existing one.

label: designed to be hosted on the JVM
citation: Hickey, R. (2020). A History of Clojure. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), 1-46.
quote: Clojure is intentionally hosted, in that it compiles to and runs on the runtime of another language, such as the JVM.
note: Influence by the platform route. Also clojure.org/about/rationale: 'Clojure is the language, JVM the platform.' The influence is the Java platform/runtime rather than Java-the-language's design.

label: ML began as LCF's meta-language, implemented in Lisp
citation: MacQueen, D., Harper, R. & Reppy, J. (2020). The History of Standard ML. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 86.
quote: Lisp was the language in which the Stanford LCF system was implemented and also served as its "meta-language." / LCF/ML was implemented by translation into Stanford Lisp code.
note: Influence by the implementation route. Label revised to match the source. The paper credits ISWIM (not Lisp) with ML's basic language framework; Lisp's role was as Stanford LCF's earlier metalanguage, ML's implementation host, and the language all designers knew, and it notes Lisp's dynamic typing as its main drawback.

label: language defined in itself (Lisp's eval)
citation: Kay, A. C. (1993). The Early History of Smalltalk. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: I could hardly believe how beautiful and wonderful the idea of LISP was [McCarthy 1960]. / I had originally made the boast because McCarthy's self-describing LISP interpreter was written in itself.
note: Label revised to match the source. Kay credits Lisp heavily, but the full text (searched end to end) never mentions garbage collection and does not credit Lisp with Smalltalk's live environment; what he credits is Lisp's meta-circular, self-describing interpreter idea.

label: unified Maclisp line
citation: Steele, G. L., Jr. & Gabriel, R. P. (1993). The Evolution of Lisp. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: Common Lisp originated in an attempt to focus the work of several implementation groups, each of which was constructing successor implementations of MacLisp for different computers.
note: Section 2.10.1; Steele edited Common Lisp: The Language and Gabriel was on the core design group. URL is a course mirror of the paper.

label: Lisp macros; generic functions (CLOS precedent)
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012). Julia: A Fast Dynamic Language for Technical Computing. arXiv:1209.5145.
quote: Generic functions have appeared in several object systems in the past, notably CLOS [15] and Dylan [28].
note: The paper goes on to distinguish Julia (generic functions as the primary abstraction, like Cecil/Diesel) and says it avoids some 'overly permissive' CLOS features. The Julia manual's Metaprogramming page (docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/metaprogramming/) says 'The strongest legacy of Lisp in the Julia language is its metaprogramming support.', and the 2012 manifesto wants 'true macros like Lisp'; both credit Lisp in general, not Common Lisp specifically.

label: functional core, without lists and brackets
citation: Landin, P. J. (1966). The Next 700 Programming Languages. Communications of the ACM 9(3), 157-165.
quote: ISWIM can be looked on as an attempt to deliver LISP from its eponymous commitment to lists, its reputation for hand-to-mouth storage allocation, the hardware dependent flavor of its pedagogy, its heavy bracketing, and its compromises with tradition.
note: Section 6. The PDF is an OCR scan ('IswI~', 'LisP fronI'); the quote fixes only the OCR errors.

label: Lisp without parentheses
citation: Solomon, C., Harvey, B., Kahn, K., Lieberman, H., Miller, M. L., Minsky, M., Papert, A. & Silverman, B. (2020). History of Logo. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 79.
quote: Logo is, first of all, a dialect of Lisp. / Lay people have often singled out parentheses as their reason not to program in Lisp. Logo avoids this controversial notation.
note: The paper explains that fixed procedure arity is what lets Logo drop most parentheses, and calls the choice of Lisp the most important aspect of Logo's design. Cynthia Solomon is one of Logo's original designers.

label: early SMP sketches (with APL)
citation: Wolfram, S. (2013). There Was a Time before Mathematica... Stephen Wolfram Writings.
quote: ones like LISP and APL. At first as I sketched out SMP, my designs looked a lot like what I'd seen in those languages. ... I started just trying to invent everything myself.
note: Label revised to match the source. About SMP, Mathematica's predecessor. Wolfram names LISP as a starting point he then moved away from; I found no designer source saying Mathematica's symbolic expressions come from Lisp S-expressions (Wolfram's 'Fast Introduction for Programmers' page on symbolic expressions does not mention Lisp).

label: closures, lexical scope
citation: Ihaka, R. (1998). R: Past and Future History. Interface '98 (Computing Science and Statistics).
quote: The two fundamental differences result from R's Scheme heritage. / In R we allow functions to access to the variables which were in effect when the function was defined
note: The two differences are lexical scoping and memory management (garbage collection); Ihaka also says R began from 'a small Scheme-like interpreter'. The 1996 Ihaka & Gentleman JCGS paper was not fetched (paywalled).

label: first-class functions
citation: Eich, B. (2008, April 3). Popularity. brendaneich.com.
quote: I'm not proud, but I'm happy that I chose Scheme-ish first-class functions and Self-ish (albeit singular) prototypes as the main ingredients.
note: The same post: 'I was recruited to Netscape with the promise of "doing Scheme" in the browser.'

label: closures, first-class functions
citation: Ierusalimschy, R., de Figueiredo, L. H. & Celes, W. (2007). The Evolution of Lua. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: initially, Scheme was just a language in the background, but later it became increasingly important as a source of inspiration
note: Later feature: anonymous functions and closures arrived in Lua 3.1 (1998), full lexical scoping in Lua 5.0 (2003).

label: multiple assignment and returns
citation: Ierusalimschy, R., de Figueiredo, L. H. & Celes, W. (2007). The Evolution of Lua. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: From CLU we took multiple assignment and multiple returns from function calls.
note: Lua 1.0 (1993); the same paper names Modula (control structures), C++ (local declarations), SNOBOL and Awk (tables) and C.

label: associative arrays (tables)
citation: Ierusalimschy, R., de Figueiredo, L. H. & Celes, W. (2007). The Evolution of Lua. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: From SNOBOL and Awk we took associative arrays, which we called tables
note: Lua 1.0 (1993). SNOBOL is credited jointly; the link is drawn from AWK, the language Lua's authors used.

label: multi-way arrays, consistent operations
citation: Becker, R. A. (1994). A Brief History of S. AT&T Bell Laboratories.
quote: From APL we borrowed the concept of the multi-way array (although we did not make it our basic data structure), and the overall consistency of operations.
note: Becker also credits APL for being typeless (no declarations) and for careful handling of boundary cases such as zero-length vectors.

label: some APL ideas (Wolfram)
citation: Wolfram, S. (2012, May 14). Answer to 'Have you ever worked with APL or J or the K/Q programming languages...?' (Reddit AMA), Stephen Wolfram Q&A.
quote: APL had some really interesting ideas, some of which have shown up in Mathematica.
note: Label revised to match the source. Wolfram says he studied APL while designing SMP but does not name which ideas carried over; he contrasts APL's symbols with Mathematica's English-word names. His 2013 'There Was a Time before Mathematica' also lists APL among languages his early SMP sketches resembled.

label: Iverson's ASCII successor
citation: Iverson, K. E. (1991). A Personal View of APL. IBM Systems Journal 30(4).
quote: The features of J that distinguish it from most other APL dialects include: / A spelling scheme that uses ASCII characters in one- or two-letter words.
note: Iverson also says work on J began in summer 1989 after he discussed his goals with Arthur Whitney (Roger Hui was the main implementer).

label: Whitney's APL line, in ASCII
citation: Cantrill, B. (2009). A Conversation with Arthur Whitney. ACM Queue.
quote: Yes, at Morgan Stanley I did use the APL characters, but on my next iteration, K, which was in '92, I gave up on those characters.
note: Whitney describes the line APL, then his own Morgan Stanley APL (A+), then K. The interview supports APL to K; it does not cover q/kdb+, and 'terse' is a description of K, not something it says was transferred.

label: S-like syntax and features
citation: Ihaka, R. (1998). R: Past and Future History. Interface '98 (Computing Science and Statistics).
quote: Since we were both very familiar with S, it seemed natural to use an S-like syntax. / we found ourselves adopting more and more features from S.
note: The syntax is stated explicitly. Data structures are not attributed to S by name (Ihaka says only 'more and more features from S'), so the label slightly over-specifies.

label: built to call Fortran's LINPACK/EISPACK routines
citation: Moler, C. (2015, 15 June). Algol 60, PL/0 and MATLAB. Cleve's Corner, MathWorks blog.
quote: I wanted my students to have access to LINPACK and EISPACK without writing Fortran programs.
note: Influence by the implementation route. Implementation link: MATLAB was a front-end to Fortran libraries.

label: syntax via Wirth's PL/0
citation: Moler, C. (2015, 15 June). Algol 60, PL/0 and MATLAB. Cleve's Corner, MathWorks blog.
quote: Consequently, the syntax of the original MATLAB is that of PL/0.
note: PL/0 is the small Pascal-like language in Wirth's 'Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs'.

label: familiar mathematical notation
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want a language that's homoiconic, with true macros like Lisp, but with obvious, familiar mathematical notation like Matlab.
note: Label revised to match the source. The Julia manual (Noteworthy differences) says 'Although MATLAB users may find Julia's syntax familiar, Julia is not a MATLAB clone.' The manual describes 'end'-terminated blocks only in its Python and C/C++ sections and never ties them to MATLAB, so the 'end blocks' part is undocumented.

label: general-purpose ease (2012 manifesto)
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want something as usable for general programming as Python
note: Python is a stated design goal ('as usable as'), not a source of specific borrowed features.

label: statistics (2012 manifesto)
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want something as usable for general programming as Python, as easy for statistics as R
note: R is a stated design goal for ease of statistics, not a source of specific borrowed features.

label: interactive front-end to Fortran statistical routines
citation: Becker, R. A. (1994). A Brief History of S. AT&T Bell Laboratories.
quote: a large, well-documented Fortran library known as SCS (Statistical Computing Subroutines) ... we simply wanted an interactive interface to the algorithms in the SCS library.
note: Influence by the implementation route. Becker, one of the designers of S, also says S itself was implemented in Fortran (via Ratfor and M4) and later had a .Fortran interface.

label: first written in Fortran
citation: Uprichard, E., Burrows, R. & Byrne, D. (2008). SPSS as an 'inscription device': from causality to description? The Sociological Review (Goldsmiths Research Online preprint).
quote: The first versions of SPSS available in the UK were written in Fortran, so users still required quite high level programming skills.
note: Influence by the implementation route. S. Simon's PMean blog (2014) also says 'SPSS was originally written in FORTRAN'. The CHM page for Nie's 1986 oral history has no Fortran mention, and no primary statement by Nie, Bent or Hull was found.

label: early SAS partly written in PL/I
citation: Simon, S. (n.d.). History of SAS. PMean blog.
quote: In 1985, the millions of lines of SAS code (mostly Pl/1, FORTRAN, and IBM Assembler) were translated into C
note: Influence by the implementation route. No source documents PL/I influencing SAS statement syntax. Only an implementation link is documented: early SAS was written partly in PL/I, as this blog and Wikipedia 'SAS (software)' both say. The syntax claim appears to rest on resemblance.

label: Mata's C-like syntax
citation: StataCorp (current release). Stata Mata Reference Manual, [M-2] syntax: Mata language grammar and syntax.
quote: Mata is a C-like compiled-into-pseudocode language with matrix extensions and runtime linking.
note: Later feature: Mata was added in Stata 9 (2005); Stata's command and ado language is not C-like. This applies to Mata, Stata's matrix language added in Stata 9, not to Stata's ado/command language. StataCorp's Stata 9 page also says Mata is 'C-like'.

label: algebraic-language precedent; Backus on the committee
citation: de Beer, H. T. (2006). The History of the ALGOL Effort (MSc thesis, TU Eindhoven), citing Perlis (1978) and Bemer (1969); and Perlis, A. J. & Samelson, K. (1958). Preliminary report: International Algebraic Language. CACM 1(12).
quote: Choosing FORTRAN as basis for their proposal would only increase the dominant position of IBM.
note: Precedent and foil, not a design source: the 1958 report cites 'experience with several successful, working problem oriented languages' without naming FORTRAN, Backus sat on the committee, and the American subcommittee deliberately did not base its proposal on FORTRAN. Drawn dotted; the analysis reports a check without this link.

label: ALGOL 60 as its base
citation: Richards, M. (2013). How BCPL evolved from CPL. The Computer Journal (author's PDF).
quote: The designers of CPL were strongly influenced by ALGOL 60 but wished to extend it to make it more efficient and usable for a wider variety of applications.
note: Richards worked on CPL at Cambridge before designing BCPL.

label: CPL minus the hard parts
citation: Richards, M. (c. 2012). How BCPL evolved from CPL. Author's version, University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory.
quote: BCPL is essentially just CPL with all the difficult bits removed and with just a few extensions.

label: cut-down BCPL (Thompson)
citation: Richards, M. (c. 2012). How BCPL evolved from CPL. Author's version, University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory.
quote: Thompson designed a cut down variant of BCPL he called B which was later extended by Ritchie resulting in C

label: B plus types
citation: Ritchie, D. M. (1993). The Development of the C Language. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: B can be thought of as C without types; more accurately, it is BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain.

label: successor, an orthogonal redesign
citation: Lindsey, C. H. (1996). A History of ALGOL 68. In History of Programming Languages II (HOPL-II), ACM Press / Addison-Wesley.
quote: ALGOL 68 clearly grew out of ALGOL 60, but many other language developments were taking place at that time
note: Lindsey was a member of IFIP WG 2.1, which took over responsibility for ALGOL 60 and produced ALGOL X / ALGOL 68.

label: if…fi, case…esac
citation: Computerworld (2009). The A-Z of Programming Languages: Bourne shell, or sh (interview with Steve Bourne). Computerworld Australia / Computerwoche.
quote: At Cambridge I had worked on the language ALGOL68 with Mike Guy. ... There was a reason that I put the ALGOL-like syntax in there.
note: Bourne explains that every compound statement got a unique closing token (if…fi, while…do…done) because matching C braces was hard to read; the interview contrasts the shell's 'ALGOL68-like syntax' with C shell's C-style syntax.

label: type composition (Ritchie)
citation: Ritchie, D. M. (1993). The Development of the C Language. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: The scheme of type composition adopted by C owes considerable debt to Algol 68, although it did not, perhaps, emerge in a form that Algol's adherents would approve of.

label: operator overloading, declarations anywhere
citation: Stroustrup, B. (1993). A History of C++: 1979–1991. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: only C, Simula, Algol68, and in one case BCPL left noticeable traces in C++ as released in 1985.
note: Stroustrup credits Algol68 for operator overloading and declarations anywhere in a block.

label: extension of ALGOL 60
citation: Nygaard, K. & Dahl, O.-J. (1978). The Development of the SIMULA Languages. History of Programming Languages (HOPL-I), ACM SIGPLAN Notices 13(8).
quote: By far the most important language ancestor of SIMULA I is of course ALGOL 60 itself.
note: The designers describe SIMULA as 'an extension of ALGOL' built on ALGOL 60 compilers; the word 'superset' itself does not appear in the paper.

label: precursor, via ALGOL W
citation: Wirth, N. (2021). 50 Years of Pascal. Communications of the ACM 64(3).
quote: Like its precursor Algol 60, Pascal featured a precise definition and a few, perspicuous basic elements.
note: Label revised to match the source. Wirth confirms ALGOL 60 as Pascal's precursor (via ALGOL W), but attributes the structured-programming influence to Dijkstra's discipline, not to ALGOL 60.

label: modules
citation: Wirth, N. (2021). 50 Years of Pascal. Communications of the ACM 64(3).
quote: Modules with type consistency checking across boundaries were indeed the primary extension of Pascal's first successor Modula-2 (for modular language, 1979).

label: simplified successor
citation: Wirth, N. (1988). From Modula to Oberon. Software: Practice and Experience 18(7).
quote: The programming language Oberon is the result of a concentrated effort increase the power of Modula-2 and simultaniously to reduce its complexity.
note: Quoted from an online transcription that contains typos; the paper also says Oberon evolved from Modula by a few additions and several subtractions.

label: safety, objects
citation: Cardelli, L., Donahue, J., Glassman, L., Jordan, M., Kalsow, B. & Nelson, G. (1989). Modula-3 Report (revised). DEC Systems Research Center, Research Report 52.
quote: Modula-3 descends from Mesa, Modula-2, Cedar, and Modula-2+. ... It adds objects and classes, exception handling, garbage collection, lightweight processes (or threads), and the isolation of unsafe features.
note: Modula-2 is one of several named ancestors (Mesa, Cedar, Modula-2+).

label: Pascal-family base
citation: US Department of Defense (1983). Reference Manual for the Ada Programming Language (ANSI/MIL-STD-1815A), §1.3 Design Goals and Sources.
quote: …influenced this language in several respects, although to a lesser degree than did the Pascal family.
note: The manual names the Pascal family as Ada's main source; ALGOL 68, Simula, Alphard and CLU as lesser ones.

label: Object Pascal
citation: Cantù, M. (n.d.). Essential Pascal, Chapter 1 (history of the Pascal language). marcocantu.com.
quote: After 9 versions of Turbo and Borland Pascal compilers, which gradually extended the language, Borland released Delphi in 1995, turning Pascal into a visual programming language.
note: Cantù is a long-time Delphi author (now Embarcadero's Delphi product manager); Embarcadero's current docs call the language 'Delphi'/'Object Pascal' but give no lineage sentence.

label: written in WEB, Knuth's Pascal-based system
citation: Knuth, D. E. (1982). TeX82 (tex.web), §1 Introduction. Copy in Xerox PARC Cedar archive, Computer History Museum.
quote: The \PASCAL\ program that follows is the definition of \TeX82, a standard version of \TeX\ that is designed to be highly portable
note: Influence by the implementation route. The same introduction says the documentation 'is written in the WEB language, which is at a higher level than PASCAL'.

label: the scientific half
citation: Meil, D. (2023). Lessons from PL/I: A Most Ambitious Programming Language. BLOG@CACM, Communications of the ACM.
quote: PL/I was designed by IBM with the goal of bringing together the power of 3 different programming languages: FORTRAN (1954), ALGOL (1958), and COBOL (1959).
note: Radin's HOPL paper (primary) could not be opened (ACM DL returned 403). Wikipedia, citing the NPL report, says IBM first hoped to extend Fortran with commercial features. ALGOL was a third input, so 'half' simplifies.

label: the business half
citation: Meil, D. (2023). Lessons from PL/I: A Most Ambitious Programming Language. BLOG@CACM, Communications of the ACM.
quote: PL/I was designed by IBM with the goal of bringing together the power of 3 different programming languages: FORTRAN (1954), ALGOL (1958), and COBOL (1959).
note: The same post calls COBOL 'The business programming language'. Wikipedia, citing Radin (1978), says 'Competitiveness with COBOL's record handling and report writing was required.' The primary was not accessible.

label: COBOL-like keyword statements
citation: SAP Community blog (2021). ABAP: Past, Present, Future. blogs.sap.com (author not shown).
quote: The ABAP syntax was heavily influenced by COBOL: keywords followed by parameters.
note: The only sources found are an SAP Community blog with no author shown and an uncited Wikipedia remark that ABAP's statement syntax 'originates in COBOL'. No SAP designer or official documentation states it, so the claim is weakly attested and may rest on resemblance.

label: record types (via Hoare, ALGOL W)
citation: Martini, S. (2015). Several types of types in programming languages. arXiv:1510.03726 (HaPoC 2015).
quote: Records are not a new idea—the concept was introduced in 'business oriented languages', FLOWMATIC first, then COBOL.
note: Martini traces the chain: Hoare's record proposal was implemented in ALGOL W, 'an important precursor of Pascal'. The link is indirect (COBOL → Hoare → ALGOL W → Pascal), and FLOW-MATIC came before COBOL. Hoare's own text was not checked.

label: C plus classes
citation: Stroustrup, B. (1993). A History of C++: 1979–1991. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: only C, Simula, Algol68, and in one case BCPL left noticeable traces in C++ as released in 1985.

label: classes, virtual functions
citation: Stroustrup, B. (1993). A History of C++: 1979–1991. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: only C, Simula, Algol68, and in one case BCPL left noticeable traces in C++ as released in 1985.

label: templates from Ada generics; exceptions
feature_evidence: widely described (Stroustrup's Design and Evolution of C++), not in the cited source
citation: Stroustrup, B. (1993). A History of C++: 1979–1991. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: The post-1985 evolution of C++ shows the influence of ideas from Ada, Clu, and ML.
note: Label made specific; the features are widely described but not stated in the cited source. Label limited to the documented claim. Stroustrup names Ada, CLU and ML together for C++ after 1985 and does not tie templates or exceptions to Ada; he traces exception handling to Brian Randell's fault-tolerance work at Newcastle. Drawn dotted, like CLU → C++, because the source gives no strength.

label: parameterized types, exceptions
feature_evidence: widely described, not in the cited source
citation: Stroustrup, B. (1993). A History of C++: 1979–1991. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), HOPL-II.
quote: The post-1985 evolution of C++ shows the influence of ideas from Ada, Clu, and ML.
note: Label made specific; the features are widely described but not stated in the cited source. Label limited to the documented claim (same sentence as Ada → C++). Drawn dotted because the source gives no strength.

label: C plus messages
citation: Apple Inc. (2014). Programming with Objective-C. Apple Developer Documentation Archive.
quote: It's a superset of the C programming language and provides object-oriented capabilities and a dynamic runtime. Objective-C inherits the syntax, primitive types, and flow control statements of C

label: Smalltalk-like messaging syntax
citation: Cox, B. J., Naroff, S. & Hsu, H. (2020). The Origins of Objective-C at PPI/Stepstone and Its Evolution at NeXT. Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 4 (HOPL IV).
quote: Cox quickly wrote up the Object-Oriented Pre-Compiler (OOPC) that would translate a Smalltalk-like syntax into C.
note: The abstract (co-written by Cox) says 'Smalltalk-like syntax' but does not use the word messaging. Apple's 'Object-Oriented Programming with Objective-C' says its additions to C 'are mostly based on Smalltalk'. Wikipedia states 'Smalltalk-style message passing'.

label: a more pragmatic C (Kelley)
citation: Kelley, A. (2016). Introduction to the Zig Programming Language. andrewkelley.me (8 February 2016).
quote: My goal is to create a new programming language that is more pragmatic than C.
note: The post also stresses C interop and gradual migration of C projects to Zig.

label: C-style expression syntax
citation: The Go Authors (n.d.). Frequently Asked Questions: 'What are Go's ancestors?'. go.dev.
quote: Go is mostly in the C family (basic syntax), with significant input from the Pascal/Modula/Oberon family (declarations, packages), plus some ideas from languages inspired by Tony Hoare's CSP, such as Newsqueak and Limbo (concurrency).

label: declarations, packages
citation: The Go Authors (n.d.). Frequently Asked Questions: 'What are Go's ancestors?'. go.dev.
quote: Go is mostly in the C family (basic syntax), with significant input from the Pascal/Modula/Oberon family (declarations, packages), plus some ideas from languages inspired by Tony Hoare's CSP, such as Newsqueak and Limbo (concurrency).

label: channels, goroutines (via Alef, Limbo)
citation: The Go Authors (n.d.). Frequently Asked Questions: 'What are Go's ancestors?'. go.dev.
quote: Go is mostly in the C family (basic syntax), with significant input from the Pascal/Modula/Oberon family (declarations, packages), plus some ideas from languages inspired by Tony Hoare's CSP, such as Newsqueak and Limbo (concurrency).
note: Alef and Limbo, Pike's intermediate languages, are not drawn as nodes.

label: safe C dialect
citation: Jim, T., Morrisett, G., Grossman, D., Hicks, M., Cheney, J. & Wang, Y. (2002). Cyclone: A safe dialect of C. USENIX Annual Technical Conference.
quote: Cyclone is a safe dialect of C. It has been designed from the ground up to prevent the buffer overflows, format string attacks, and memory management errors that are common in C programs

label: region-based memory (lifetimes)
citation: The Rust Project (n.d.). The Rust Reference, Appendix 'Influences'. doc.rust-lang.org.
quote: ML Kit, Cyclone: region based memory management

label: RAII, move semantics, monomorphization
citation: The Rust Project (n.d.). The Rust Reference, Appendix 'Influences'. doc.rust-lang.org.
quote: C++: references, RAII, smart pointers, move semantics, monomorphization, memory model

label: algebraic data types, pattern matching
citation: The Rust Project (n.d.). The Rust Reference, Appendix 'Influences'. doc.rust-lang.org.
quote: SML, OCaml: algebraic data types, pattern matching, type inference, semicolon statement separation
note: OCaml was also the language of Rust's first compiler (implementation).

label: traits from type classes
citation: The Rust Project (n.d.). The Rust Reference, Appendix 'Influences'. doc.rust-lang.org.
quote: Haskell (GHC): typeclasses, type families

label: named parameters, ARC, Obj-C interop
citation: Swift.org (n.d.). About Swift. swift.org.
quote: Swift also borrows from other languages, for instance named parameters brought forward from Objective-C are expressed in a clean syntax that makes APIs in Swift easy to read and maintain.
note: For ARC, The Swift Programming Language's ARC chapter says 'Using ARC in Swift is very similar to the approach described in Transitioning to ARC Release Notes for using ARC with Objective-C.' 'Cocoa object model' was not found verbatim; swift.org only says Apple platforms include the Objective-C runtime to reach UIKit and AppKit.

label: opt-in ownership model
citation: Lattner, C. (2016, July 29). Looking back on Swift 3 and ahead to Swift 4. swift-evolution (Swift Forums).
quote: Adding an (opt-in) Cyclone/Rust inspired memory ownership model to Swift is highly desired by systems programmers
note: The Swift Ownership Manifesto (swift/docs/OwnershipManifesto.md) notes 'many similarities between shared values and Rust's concept of an immutable borrow'. Lattner's homepage lists Rust among Swift's sources of ideas. The ownership part is well supported; a general 'safety' influence is not specifically documented.

label: approachability, script-like top level
citation: Lattner, C., interviewed by Arment, M., Liss, C., & Siracusa, J. (2017). ATP Episode 205: Chris Lattner Interview Transcript. Accidental Tech Podcast.
quote: just like in Python, you can start with just print("Hello world"). You can do the exact same thing in Swift
note: Label revised to match the source. Lattner's homepage (nondot.org/sabre) lists Python among the languages Swift drew ideas from, but names no feature. The only concrete point found is approachability (script-like top-level code / progressive disclosure); 'readability' is not specified.

label: protocols akin to type classes
citation: Lattner, C., interviewed by Arment, M., Liss, C., & Siracusa, J. (2017). ATP Episode 205: Chris Lattner Interview Transcript. Accidental Tech Podcast.
quote: If you're a Haskell nerd, there is tons of Haskell concepts built in. Protocols really are just like a very similar Haskell construct, for example.
note: Label revised to match the source. Lattner does not name the construct; reading it as type classes is an inference. No Lattner or Apple source found that ties Optional to Maybe, and the Swift Generics Manifesto does not mention Haskell. Lattner's homepage lists Haskell among Swift's sources of ideas.

label: based on Ada
citation: Oracle (2005). Oracle Database PL/SQL User's Guide and Reference 10g Release 2 (10.2), Appendix C: PL/SQL Program Limits.
quote: PL/SQL is based on the programming language Ada. As a result, PL/SQL uses a variant of Descriptive Intermediate Attributed Notation for Ada (DIANA), a tree-structured intermediate language.
note: Label revised to match the source. Oracle states the Ada basis directly but does not list which features came from Ada; block syntax, packages and exceptions are Ada-like, but this source does not say they were inherited.

label: classes & objects
citation: Kay, A. C. (1993). The Early History of Smalltalk. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3) (HOPL-II).
quote: What Simula was allocating were structures very much like the instances of Sketchpad. There were descriptions that acted like masters and they could create instances, each of which was an independent entity.
note: Kay also writes of 'Simula leading to OOP' in the same paper.

label: learning by programming
citation: Kay, A. C. (1993). The Early History of Smalltalk. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3) (HOPL-II).
quote: Here were children doing real programming with a specially designed language and environment. As with Simula leading to OOP, this encounter finally hit me with what the destiny of personal computing really was going to be.
note: The quote follows Kay's account of visiting Seymour Papert, Wally Feurzeig, Cynthia Solomon and the others who built LOGO and used it with children in the Lexington schools.

label: classes, inheritance
citation: Meyer, B. (n.d.). Bio. bertrandmeyer.com (designer's own website).
quote: His experience with object technology through the Simula language, as well as early work on abstract data types and formal specification [...] provided some of the background for the development of Eiffel.
note: Third-person bio on Meyer's own site. It says 'object technology' (which in Simula means classes and inheritance) rather than naming those features. The ECMA-367 Eiffel standard does not mention Simula.

label: simpler Smalltalk: prototypes, no classes
citation: Ungar, D. & Smith, R. B. (2007). Self. Proc. HOPL III (ACM SIGPLAN History of Programming Languages).
quote: Inspired by Smith's Alternate Reality Kit [Smi87] and their years of working with Smalltalk [GR83], they wanted to improve upon Smalltalk by increasing both expressive power and simplicity, while obtaining a more concrete feel.
note: The paper also says confusion over Smalltalk-80's metaclasses 'gave us a strong push to eliminate classes when we designed Self'. The authors never call Self a Smalltalk 'dialect'.

label: syntax, minus pointers
citation: Gosling, J. & McGilton, H. (1996). The Java Language Environment: A White Paper. Sun Microsystems.
quote: keeping the Java programming language looking like C++ as far as possible results in it being a familiar language, while removing the unnecessary complexities of C++.
note: The same white paper says 'There are no explicit programmer-defined pointer data types, no pointer arithmetic' and, in section 2 (simple-familiar.html), 'Java has no pointer data types.'

label: OO ideas; Smalltalk VM know-how
citation: Gosling, J. & McGilton, H. (1996). The Java Language Environment: A White Paper. Sun Microsystems.
quote: Design and architecture decisions drew from a variety of languages such as Eiffel, SmallTalk, Objective C, and Cedar/Mesa.
note: Label revised to match the source. The white paper credits Smalltalk only in general terms and does not link it to the VM or GC. In 'A Conversation with James Gosling' (ACM Queue, 2004, https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=1017013) Gosling says a p-code translator 'formed the core of the design' and that he then consulted 'people like Peter Deutsch who had worked on the Smalltalk VMs'.

label: type safety, exceptions, GC
citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.
quote: Java certainly demonstrated the value of type safety, exception handling, and garbage collection in a mainstream programming language. [...] Many programming languages influenced C#. Java was one of them, but C++ and Delphi also influenced our design.
note: Label revised to match the source. Hejlsberg confirms the Java influence and names type safety, exceptions and GC (the interviewer calls Java a 'managed platform'). He does not mention classes or interfaces.

label: C-family syntax
citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.
quote: Many programming languages influenced C#. Java was one of them, but C++ and Delphi also influenced our design.
note: Label revised to match the source. Microsoft's C# overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/tour-of-csharp/overview) says 'C# is in the C family of languages' and that its syntax is familiar to C/C++ users. No source found that credits operator overloading to C++.

label: properties, events, is/as (same designer, Hejlsberg)
feature_evidence: widely described, not in the cited source
citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.
quote: C++ and Delphi also influenced our design. If I had to call out a few of the differences between C# and Java [...] I might mention C#'s unified type system [...], first class support for properties and events, delegate types
note: Label made specific; the features are widely described but not stated in the cited source. Label limited to the documented claim: Hejlsberg names Delphi as an influence and lists properties and events among C#'s differences from Java, without attributing them to Delphi. The Artima interview 'Delegates, Components, and Simplexity' (2003) discusses first-class properties and events but does not mention Delphi. Drawn dotted because the source gives no strength.

label: classes, JVM interop
citation: Odersky, M. (2006). A Brief History of Scala. Artima Weblogs.
quote: Scala is not an extension of Java, but it is completely interoperable with it. Scala translates to Java bytecodes, and the efficiency of its compiled programs usually equals Java's.
note: Odersky et al., 'An Overview of the Scala Programming Language' (2006) adds that 'Scala adopts a large part of the concepts and syntactic conventions of Java and C#.'

label: functional style (ML family)
citation: Odersky, M., Spoon, L. & Venners, B. (2008). Programming in Scala, 1st ed., ch. 1 'Scala's roots'. Artima.
quote: Its approach to functional programming is quite similar in spirit to the ML family of languages, which has SML, OCaml, and F# as prominent members.
note: Label revised to match the source. The designers link Scala's FP style to ML but never credit pattern matching to ML specifically. Emir, Odersky & Williams, 'Matching Objects With Patterns' (2006), opens by noting that 'A number of functional languages are built on patterns... Examples are SML, OCaml or Haskell.'

label: type classes
citation: Odersky, M., Spoon, L. & Venners, B. (2008). Programming in Scala, 1st ed., ch. 1 'Scala's roots'. Artima.
quote: Scala's implicit parameters were motivated by Haskell's type classes; they achieve analogous results in a more classical object-oriented setting.
note: Also in Odersky et al., 'An Overview of the Scala Programming Language' (2006): 'Views have been influenced by Haskell's type classes.'

label: indentation syntax
citation: Odersky, M. (2019). Allow significant indentation syntax (pull request #7083). scala/scala3 (Dotty) repository, GitHub.
quote: The most widely taught language is now (or will be soon, in any case) Python, which is indentation based.
note: Python is one of several precedents in Odersky's rationale, alongside Haskell, F#, Elm, Agda, Idris, Markdown and YAML. He cites it to show the style is familiar, not as a direct model. The Scala 3 reference page on optional braces names no other language.

label: classes, 100% JVM interop
citation: JetBrains (n.d.). FAQ. Kotlin Documentation, kotlinlang.org.
quote: Kotlin is 100% interoperable with the Java programming language, and major emphasis has been placed on making sure that your existing codebase can interact properly with Kotlin.
note: The same FAQ lists Java first among Kotlin's inspirations.

label: val/var, name: Type, primary constructors, object singletons
feature_evidence: widely described, not in the cited source
citation: JetBrains (n.d.). FAQ. Kotlin Documentation, kotlinlang.org.
quote: Kotlin is inspired by existing languages such as Java, C#, JavaScript, Scala, and Groovy.
note: Label made specific; the features are widely described but not stated in the cited source. Label limited to the documented claim: the FAQ names Scala as an inspiration without naming features. Drawn dotted because the FAQ gives no strength.

label: extension functions (Breslav talk)
citation: JetBrains (n.d.). FAQ. Kotlin Documentation, kotlinlang.org.
quote: Kotlin is inspired by existing languages such as Java, C#, JavaScript, Scala, and Groovy.
note: Feature evidence is a slide title in Breslav's 2022 talk ('Extensions in C# and Scala'); drawn dotted. The current extensions page (and the Kotlin 1.9 docs) never mention C# or Gosu, and I could not reach an archived official copy of the old 'similar to C# and Gosu' wording because the Wayback Machine is blocked. Breslav's 2022 talk 'Shoulders of Giants' (SlideShare) has a slide titled 'Extensions in C# and Scala'. No source credits properties to C#.

label: pipelines, but of objects
citation: Snover, J. (2002). Monad Manifesto. Microsoft (republished at jsnover.com).
quote: Instead of piping unstructured text, we pipe .Net objects.
note: The manifesto also says MSH uses 'the functions and syntax of the POSIX Shell model ... as a starting point' and criticizes the text-based UNIX pipeline.

label: C#-like syntax (glide path to C#)
citation: Snover, J. (2002). Monad Manifesto. Microsoft (republished at jsnover.com).
quote: These are then modified and expanded upon to either improve the programming experience, take advantage of new functionality or provide a glide path to C#.
note: Label revised to match the source. 'These' are the POSIX-shell-based script constructs. Cmdlets are written 'in C#, VB.NET, COBOL, etc'. The .NET objects come from the CLR platform, not from C#, so the C# link is the cmdlet language and a deliberate syntactic glide path.

label: let/where, expression language
citation: MacQueen, D., Harper, R. & Reppy, J. (2020). The History of Standard ML. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 86.
quote: The basic framework of the language design was inspired by Peter Landin's ISWIM language from the mid 1960s [1966b], which was, in turn, a sugared syntax for Church's lambda calculus.
note: The same paper describes ISWIM as an applied call-by-value lambda calculus 'with syntactic sugar (e.g., "where" and "let" declaration constructs)', and says ML followed ISWIM in strict evaluation and allowing impure features.

label: ISWIM's applicative core, via PAL, SASL and KRC
citation: Turner, D. A. (2012). Some History of Functional Programming Languages. Invited lecture, Trends in Functional Programming (TFP 2012), St Andrews.
quote: ISWIM inspired PAL (Evans 1968) at MIT / a simple DL based on the applicative subset of PAL / Miranda is essentially SASL plus algebraic types and the polymorphic type discipline of Milner (1978).
note: Turner's chain is ISWIM, then PAL, then SASL, then KRC ('a miniaturized version of SASL', where guards first appeared), then Miranda. He also credits ISWIM directly for having no explicit lambdas and for the offside rule.

label: Hindley-Milner types
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Milner's polymorphic type system for ML would prove to be particularly influential (Milner, 1978; Damas and Milner, 1982). / incorporated many innovations to the core Hindley-Milner type system, especially type classes
note: The paper also says Miranda already had a Hindley-Milner type system, so this influence also reached Haskell through Miranda. Type classes generalized SML's equality type variables.

label: lazy, pure (open rewrite)
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Of all the lazy languages under development, David Turner's Miranda was by far the most mature. / After a brief and cordial interchange, Turner declined. / It should be freely available.
note: The committee asked Turner whether Miranda could be the starting point, and he declined. Miranda's license required permission before distributing an implementation or a substantially copied language, and a freely available language was one of Haskell's stated goals.

label: dialect + objects
citation: OCaml.org (n.d.). About OCaml / history. Official OCaml website.
quote: It was inspired by a long line of research into ML / The modern OCaml emerged in 1996, when Didier Rémy and Jérôme Vouillon implemented a powerful and elegant object system.
note: This is the official site rather than a paper. It traces ML to LCF and Caml to INRIA in 1987. Note that it dates LCF/ML to 1972, while other sources say 1973.

label: OCaml for .NET
citation: Syme, D. (2020). The Early History of F#. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 75.
quote: The early conception of F# was simple: to bring the benefits of OCaml to .NET and .NET to OCaml
note: The working name was 'Caml.NET', and the 2002 announcement called F# 'an implementation of the core of the Caml programming language for the .NET Framework'. Syme notes it was never fully compatible with any OCaml version.

label: pipe operator |>
citation: Valim, J. (2018). Post in 'Which language first introduced the pipe operator?'. Elixir Forum.
quote: Almost sure we got it from F# but somebody pointed early on that it existed in ML before that.
note: The |> operator itself dates from Isabelle/ML (1994).

label: functional; 'similar to F#' (Microsoft)
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). Power Query M formula language. Microsoft Learn.
quote: The M language is a functional, case-sensitive language similar to F#.
note: Microsoft states a similarity, not an influence. The M spec introduction (m-spec-introduction) calls M 'mostly pure, higher-order, dynamically typed, partially lazy', models its evaluation on spreadsheets, and does not mention F#.

label: pipe |>, via magrittr; native in R 4.1
citation: Bache, S. M. & Wickham, H. (n.d.). Introducing magrittr (package vignette), CRAN; and Tierney, L. (n.d.). Native pipe design note (PIPE.md), R Project SVN.
quote: a prime example is the |> operator used extensively in F# (to say the least) and indeed this – along with Unix pipes – served as a motivation for developing the magrittr package.
note: Influence by the library route. Library link: R core's design note for the native pipe (R 4.1) cites magrittr, not F#.

label: LAMBDA (MSR functional-programming research)
citation: Microsoft Research Podcast (2021). Advancing Excel as a programming language with Andy Gordon and Simon Peyton Jones.
quote: the North Star of mainstream functional programming languages
note: Later feature: LAMBDA (2020) came from Microsoft Research's functional-programming work with Haskell co-designer Simon Peyton Jones; Haskell itself is not named as the source.

label: Bourne Again
citation: Ramey, C. & Fox, B. (current ed.). Bash Reference Manual, §1.1 "What is Bash?". Free Software Foundation (copy hosted by Chet Ramey, Case Western Reserve University).
quote: The name is an acronym for the 'Bourne-Again SHell', a pun on Stephen Bourne, the author of the direct ancestor of the current Unix shell sh
note: Same section: 'Bash is largely compatible with sh and incorporates useful features from the Korn shell ksh and the C shell csh.' gnu.org refused automated fetching, so the maintainer's mirror was used.

label: shell features (Wall names sh)
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: It combines (in the author's opinion, anyway) some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh, so people familiar with those languages should have little difficulty with it.
note: In 1987 'sh' meant the Bourne shell; the same page adds 'Language historians will also note some vestiges of csh, Pascal, and even BASIC-PLUS.' The current perl(1) at perldoc.perl.org says 'sed, awk, and sh' and drops C.

label: awk-style text scanning, reports
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: Perl is a interpreted language optimized for scanning arbitrary text files, extracting information from those text files, and printing reports based on that information.
note: Same DESCRIPTION: Perl 'combines ... some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh' and 'There are also translators to turn your sed and awk scripts into perl scripts.' The page names awk as a source but does not single out its patterns; the regex side is equally credited to sed.

label: C-like syntax
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: Expression syntax corresponds quite closely to C expression syntax.
note: The same page lists C first among 'the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh'.

label: C-like syntax
citation: Aho, A. V., Kernighan, B. W. & Weinberger, P. J. (1979). Awk — A Pattern Scanning and Processing Language. Software: Practice and Experience 9(4) (copy hosted at awk.dev).
quote: The for statement is also exactly that of C
note: The paper also says 'the C increment ++ and decrement -- operators are also available' and that printf matches 'the standard I/O library used with the programming language C'. Venue taken from the file name and standard bibliographies; the PDF's first page shows only Bell Laboratories.

label: associative arrays (likened to SNOBOL4 tables)
citation: Aho, A. V., Kernighan, B. W. & Weinberger, P. J. (1979). Awk — A Pattern Scanning and Processing Language. Software: Practice and Experience 9(4) (copy hosted at awk.dev).
quote: Non-numeric array subscripts give awk a capability rather like the associative memory of Snobol tables.
note: Label revised to match the source. The designers compare the feature to SNOBOL tables but do not say they borrowed it. Aho's 2016 Simple Talk interview names grep as the main inspiration and does not mention SNOBOL.

label: SNOBOL4 patterns recast as string scanning
citation: Griswold, R. E. (1994). Icon in the Humanities. TEXT Technology 4(1), 13-19 (online version updated 1996, University of Arizona).
quote: The design of Icon was motivated by the desire to recast some features of SNOBOL4 in more general ways and to provide facilities that SNOBOL4 lacks.
note: Griswold also calls Icon 'in some ways, a successor to SNOBOL4' and says string scanning answered weaknesses in SNOBOL4's pattern matching. The Icon Version 5 Reference Manual (Griswold et al., 1981; https://gmorph.cs.arizona.edu/icon/ftp/doc/tr81_4a.pdf) says SNOBOL4-style patterns 'were replaced by the concept of string scanning'. String scanning is Icon's replacement for SNOBOL4 patterns, not something taken from SNOBOL.

label: generators (yield)
citation: Schemenauer, N., Peters, T. & Hetland, M. L. (2001). PEP 255 – Simple Generators. Python Enhancement Proposals.
quote: generators in Icon, a novel language where every expression is a generator. There are differences among these, but the basic idea is the same
note: Later feature: generators arrived in Python 2.2 (PEP 255, 2001). The Motivation section cites Icon together with Sather and CLU iterators as prior art, and the Q&A compares Python with Icon's 'return expr' semantics.

label: indentation, built-in types
citation: van Rossum, G. (2009). Early Language Design and Development. The History of Python (blog).
quote: Python's use of indentation comes directly from ABC ... Python's major data types also derive from ABC, though with some modifications.
note: The same post credits ABC with the colon before indented blocks and with tuple packing and unpacking. Guido's 1996 foreword to Programming Python says indentation 'derives directly from ABC'.

label: indentation for grouping
citation: Meertens, L. (2019). On the history of ABC (talk slides, CWI, 21 November 2019).
quote: ISWIM (Landin 1966, an expression-oriented 'paperware' language) introduced indentation for grouping
note: Meertens adds that readability was the motivation for adopting indentation in ABC: a precedent rather than a documented borrowing.

label: modules, exceptions, explicit self
citation: Kuchling, A. M. (1998). LJ Interviews Guido van Rossum. Linux Journal.
quote: the Modula-3 final report was being written there at about the same time. What I learned there showed up in Python's exception handling, modules, and the fact that methods explicitly contain "self" in their parameter list.
note: Guido credits his DEC SRC exposure to Modula-2+ and Modula-3. For classes, the Python Tutorial §9 says the class mechanism 'is a mixture of the class mechanisms found in C++ and Modula-3'.

label: class mechanism (with Modula-3)
citation: Python Software Foundation (current ed.). The Python Tutorial, §9 Classes. docs.python.org.
quote: Python's class mechanism adds classes with a minimum of new syntax and semantics. It is a mixture of the class mechanisms found in C++ and Modula-3.
note: The same section uses C++ terms (members 'public', member functions 'virtual') and credits the explicit self argument to Modula-3.

label: keywords, operator precedence
citation: Kuchling, A. M. (1998). LJ Interviews Guido van Rossum. Linux Journal.
quote: C is a second influence, second only to ABC in importance. Most of Python's keywords, such as break, continue and others, are identical to C's, as are operator priorities.
note: Guido also says early extension modules such as socket and POSIX wrap the UNIX C functions. His 1996 foreword says he 'borrowed from C too, but only its least controversial features'.

label: list comprehensions
citation: Kuchling, A. M. & Zadka, M. (2000). What's New in Python 2.0, §List Comprehensions. Python documentation.
quote: The idea of list comprehensions originally comes from the functional programming language Haskell
note: Later feature: list comprehensions arrived in Python 2.0 (2000). Same paragraph: Greg Ewing wrote the first patch and Skip Montanaro kept it up to date. The PEP 202 text was not checked.

label: joins, group-by, via pandas
citation: McKinney, W. (2010). Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python. Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2010).
quote: This is akin to a SQL join operation between two tables.
note: Influence by the library route. The paper also says 'This concept of "group by" is a built-in feature of many data-oriented languages, such as R and SQL.' The SQL influence reaches pandas, not the Python language itself.

label: data frames, via pandas
citation: McKinney, W. (2010). Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python. Proceedings of the 9th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2010).
quote: pandas provides a similarly-named DataFrame class which implements much of the functionality of its R counterpart, though with some important enhancements (namely, built-in data alignment)
note: Influence by the library route. The R influence reaches pandas, not the Python language itself.

label: C-like syntax, function names
citation: The PHP Group (current ed.). History of PHP. PHP Manual.
quote: The language was deliberately designed to resemble C in structure, making it an easy adoption for developers familiar with C, Perl, and similar languages.
note: On function names, Rasmus Lerdorf wrote on php-internals (2 Jan 2014, https://externals.io/message/70896) that 'The function names and argument order, for the most part, were taken directly from these underlying libraries', citing MySQL's C API.

label: syntax, $ variables
citation: The PHP Group (current ed.). History of PHP. PHP Manual.
quote: It had Perl-like variables, automatic interpretation of form variables, and HTML embedded syntax. The syntax itself was similar to that of Perl, albeit much more limited, simple, and somewhat inconsistent.
note: This describes PHP/FI (1995-96).

label: PHP plus gradual typing
citation: Verlaguet, J. & Menghrajani, A. (2014, March 20). Hack: a new programming language for HHVM. Engineering at Meta (Facebook Engineering blog).
quote: Hack has deep roots in PHP. In fact, most PHP files are already valid Hack files. ... Technically speaking, Hack is a 'gradually typed' language
note: This describes Hack at launch (2014); its later divergence from PHP was not checked. docs.hhvm.com returned no readable text.

label: nullable types ?T
citation: PHP RFC: Nullable Return Types (2016; implemented in PHP 7.1). wiki.php.net.
quote: I propose to use HHVM compatible syntax to declare nullable return types - ?<type>
note: Later feature: PHP 7.1 (2016).

label: everything is an object
citation: Ruby community (current ed.). About Ruby. ruby-lang.org (official site).
quote: Ruby follows the influence of the Smalltalk language by giving methods and instance variables to all of its types.
note: Label revised to match the source. The 'everything is an object' part is stated as a Smalltalk influence. Blocks are only a resemblance: the official FAQ says 'Like Smalltalk, everything in Ruby is an object, and Ruby has blocks', but the About page says 'Blocks are inspired by functional languages' (Lisp), and a 2019 recap of a Matz talk credits blocks to CLU.

label: iterators, yield
citation: AppFolio Engineering Blog (2019, July 3). Ruby's Roots and Matz's Leadership (recap of a Matz talk at Cookpad, Bristol).
quote: Matz feels that blocks are the greatest invention of Ruby (I agree.) He got the idea from a 1970s language called CLU from MIT, which called them "iterators"
note: This is a second-hand recap of Matz's talk. Matz's own ruby-list:102 post (30 Jan 1996, https://blade.ruby-lang.org/ruby-list/102) only says CLU also has iterators, not that Ruby took them from CLU. No primary attribution was found.

label: end-delimited syntax, rescue/ensure
citation: Ruby community (current ed.). About Ruby. ruby-lang.org (official site).
quote: Its creator, Yukihiro "Matz" Matsumoto, blended parts of his favorite languages (Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada, and Lisp) to form a new language
note: The influence is documented but not 'clean object model'. The 2019 AppFolio recap of a Matz talk says begin/end keywords, if/elsif/else/end 'comb indentation' and rescue/ensure/retry came from Eiffel.

label: regex, scripting
citation: Matsumoto, Y. (1999, June 4). Post on Ruby's history. ruby-talk mailing list, message 382.
quote: I knew Perl (Perl4, not Perl5), but I didn't like it really, because it had smell of toy language ... Then, I reorganized the features in Perl into class library, and implemented them.
note: The official Ruby FAQ says 'Like Perl, Ruby is good at text processing'. Regex specifically is credited to Perl only by secondary sources, e.g. twobithistory.org (2017): 'Ruby borrows much of Perl's regular expression handling and standard library.'

label: Ruby-like surface syntax
citation: Valim, J. (2016, February 26). Re: Any Erlang Devs Contemplating Elixir? erlang-questions mailing list.
quote: Elixir is not Ruby (and it could never be in the Erlang VM). Elixir also isn't about Ruby syntax (the same way Erlang isn't about Prolog syntax)
note: Valim's analogy implies a surface-syntax lineage but plays it down. No explicit designer statement of borrowing was found. Wikipedia lists Ruby under 'Influenced by' without a citation, and Valim was a Rails core team member (Code BEAM 2014 bio).

label: processes, OTP, the BEAM
citation: Elixir team (current ed.). Introduction to Mix (Mix and OTP guide). Elixir official documentation, hexdocs.
quote: OTP (Open Telecom Platform) is a set of libraries that ships with Erlang. Erlang developers use OTP to build robust, fault-tolerant applications.
note: The guide says it will show 'how many aspects from OTP integrate with Elixir, including supervision trees'. The elixir-lang.org homepage says Elixir is 'running on the battle-tested Erlang VM'.

label: syntax, pattern matching; began as Prolog with processes
citation: Armstrong, J. (2010). Talk slides, Erlang Factory SF Bay Area 2010.
quote: A Prolog interpretor for the telephony algebra … Deterministic prolog with processes
note: Slide text; Erlang's syntax and pattern matching are Prolog-derived, its concurrency model is not.

label: prototypes
citation: Eich, B. (2008). Popularity. brendaneich.com (blog).
quote: I'm happy that I chose Scheme-ish first-class functions and Self-ish (albeit singular) prototypes as the main ingredients.

label: syntax, by marketing mandate
citation: Eich, B. (2008). Popularity. brendaneich.com (blog).
quote: The diktat from upper engineering management was that the language must 'look like Java'.

label: generators and iterators
citation: Eich, B. (2006). Python and JavaScript. brendaneich.com (blog), 19 Feb 2006.
quote: This brings to mind a hot topic in my recent hacking: infusing JS with Pythonic generators and iterators, including array comprehensions.
